prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, taking atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement breakthrough with a clear, decisive credit. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the lattice light shift, and his group made the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group then took the clocks to about 1e-18 accuracy and stability and showed they work as many-body probes. The result has been confirmed independently by JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and comparisons between laboratories are now routine. That is what I ask of an instrument result: the calibration and systematics work is done, the community believes the number, and it opens new uses (relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, a likely redefinition of the second). All eight of us named the same two laureates, so the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. It also has the broadest opening support, with eight rankings, three first places and four top-three placements.
statement.case_against: Broad support is not the same as merit, and a metrology prize can look incremental to colleagues who prefer a new phase of matter or a new observational window. Hall and Hansch were already honoured in 2005 for frequency combs and precision spectroscopy, and the clock community is wider than two people (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ye's JILA collaborators and others), so a two-name credit will be read as a choice. The SI second has not yet been redefined, so critics could say the practical payoff is still to come. Three of us ranked it sixth or seventh, and I should take that seriously rather than treat it as noise.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B001) first as a genuine invention that moved routine microscopy to the sub-angstrom regime, with Rose, Haider and Urban as a clean three-person credit.
responses.response: I agree on the instrument merit, and I ranked B001 third myself. My reservation is the 1986 prize for the electron microscope, which makes this feel like a refinement of an already recognised instrument. Its value lies mostly in chemistry and materials science, and Krivanek, who built the STEM corrector, is outside the credited names. I could support it, but I do not see it beating the lattice clock on novelty of the measurement regime. Does the committee consider the corrector a new discovery in physics, or a major enabling technology?

responses.point: Olle Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B003) first and B023 second, because they give new phases of matter and a tunable platform for correlated electrons, and he ranks the lattice clock only seventh.
responses.response: I respect the case for B003. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 discovery by Jarillo-Herrero's group is a good theory-plus-experiment pairing, and it has been reproduced widely. I differ on timing and certainty. The superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, and Cao and the other early experimenters are outside the credited names, so the discovery credit is less settled than for the clock. Precision measurement is also a legitimate way for physics to advance, and it sits close to the 2005 and 2012 recognitions, so I do not think a ranking of seventh reflects its physics. I keep B003 as my first alternative and would not oppose it if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, citing 1e-18 uncertainty, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and the agreement among independent Sr, Yb and Hg clocks. She wants a two-person prize for Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree with her on the credit and on maturity. I would add a qualification. The case should not lean on a future redefinition of the second, which has not happened. It should rest on what is already demonstrated: accuracy at 1e-18, comparisons between laboratories, and height-sensitivity measurements at the centimetre scale. Our citation should therefore name the clock itself, not a promised application. As an atomic physicist she is better placed than I am to judge whether Lemonde or Ludlow have a claim that a two-name prize would unfairly pass over, and I would welcome her view on that.

responses.point: Goran Johansson ranks circuit QED (B043) first as a clean new regime of light-matter physics that underpins superconducting quantum processors, and puts the lattice clock third.
responses.response: Circuit QED is a strong result, and I take his point that it is mature and reproduced everywhere. But the 2025 prize already went to superconducting-circuit quantum tunnelling and quantum devices, so a second prize in that area soon after raises a balance question. He also shows three names, Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf, while Wallraff's experiment is part of the story, so the attribution is more contested than for the clock. I would rank it behind B024 for 2026, but I would like to hear whether he thinks that overlap is a real problem.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson ranks B003 first and B023 second, valuing a prediction followed by a discovery in nature, and he puts IceCube (B035) third while ranking the lattice clock sixth.
responses.response: I share his interest in IceCube. I ranked it second and I think the diffuse neutrino flux is firmly established. But his caveat that source identification is still only partial applies, and the credit is spread across the AMANDA and IceCube collaboration, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the three plausible names. I am not neutral on that point, since it is my own field. I would prefer to see a clearer source association before pressing it, which is why it is an alternative and not my first choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-person credit for Katori and Ye, or consider the contributions of other clock groups (for example Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley) large enough to need a different configuration.
Whether the 2005 prize for Hall and Hansch makes precision frequency metrology look already recognised, and how much weight that should carry.
How much of the clock case should rest on the expected redefinition of the second, which has not occurred.

Whether magic-angle graphene (B003) or topological insulators (B023) are mature enough, and whether the early experimental credit (Cao and co-workers) can be resolved, given they have more first-place and top-three support than I credited in my opening ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B024 from my profile. I work in astroparticle physics, so I am close to the IceCube field (B035) and the Higgs search community (B010) in subject, and I collaborate in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur, but not with the credited names. I would flag the proximity if B035 were seriously considered.
